title: The Light Spark Chain Reaction
markdown:
“Whoa, what was that!” squawked Tern the gull, wings flapping. The classroom lights flickered wildly, then winked out. A wave of gasps swept the students gathered for the energy debate. Teacher Jae stepped forward, smile strained. “Just a power hiccup,” they said, but their worried eyebrows danced.

Sana, the app designer, watched the flicker from the second row, where the projector usually lied about contrast. It was not random. A pattern, a rhythm, like a message flashing fast. One flash seemed to cause the next. The room buzzed. Dominoes: one falling, then another, faster. She remembered her app project on atomic energy, how to show a chain reaction, the one Jae had said was too abstract for a debate. These lights were cousins of that idea, and they had arrived early.

“Teacher Jae!” she called. “It’s like when one tiny thing makes a bunch of other tiny things happen — light bits causing more light to burst out.”

Jae blinked. “Are you talking about atomic fission?”

“Sort of.” She pulled up the app. “Imagine each spark is a particle. When one bumps something — boosh — it breaks and releases more. Those zoom out and bump others. More breaks. More particles. A chain.” She tapped the screen. Digital particles bounced, triggering more reactions. In the classroom the lights pulsed, a blinding flash and a dizzying dimness. The air hummed. A faint metallic smell tickled Tern’s nose. He sneezed a feather onto Leo’s notes.

“Why is it so uncontrolled?” Leo asked. “It feels like it’s going to explode.”

“That’s where control rods come in.” Sana’s face lit. “In a real reactor, special materials soak up extra particles. Polite bouncers. They stop too many things breaking apart too quickly.” She added dark bars to the simulation. As the digital rods slid in, they caught the zooming particles. The frantic flashing slowed to a gentle pulse. The classroom lights softened, wild flicker settling into a steady glow — as if the building itself had been waiting for the metaphor.

Tern tilted his head. “So if we had fluffy feathers to catch all the light bits, it wouldn’t get so wiggly?”

“Feathers, rods. Same job, different furniture,” Sana said.

Jae beamed. They did not turn it into a speech about using science safely. “You showed the start and the stop. The interesting part is both.”

The lights returned to a normal, slightly embarrassed glow. A collective sigh. The energy debate had taken an illuminating turn: someone had been arguing that reactors were just ‘big fires,’ and now even they were staring at Sana’s dark bars.

Sana smiled, a thrill of discovery, and did not wonder about other invisible forces. She saved the simulation with the rods half-in, emailed Jae the file labelled hiccup / not magic, and let Tern keep the feather that had landed on fission, because a gull’s idea of peer review is stealing the exhibit.
